Assign new respondents to the clusters of a solution

Source: R/seg_predict.R
predict.seg_cluster.Rd

Assigns new respondents (e.g. a new survey wave, a holdout sample or a short "golden question" screener) to the clusters of an existing cluster solution from seg_cluster(), and optionally returns their membership probabilities.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'seg_cluster'
predict(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  type = c("cluster", "prob"),
  rule = NULL,
  neighbors = 10,
  id = NULL,
  labels = TRUE,
  verbose = TRUE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'seg_cluster_set'
predict(object, ...)

Arguments

object

A cluster solution of class seg_cluster, e.g. from seg_cluster().

newdata

A data frame with the new respondents. It must contain the (original, unprepared) clustering variables, e.g. the same columns as the data passed to seg_prep_data(). If NULL (default), the assignment of the original sample is returned.

type

"cluster" (default) for the assigned cluster, or "prob" to add the membership probabilities (prob_cluster_1, prob_cluster_2, ...). Probabilities are available for fuzzy clustering, model-based clustering and rule = "knn".

rule

Assignment rule: NULL (default) for the rule of the clustering method (see "Assignment rules"), "centroid", "knn", or "linkage" (AGNES and DIANA only).

neighbors

Number of nearest neighbors for rule = "knn". Defaults to 10.

id

Name of an identifier column in newdata to be included in the result. Defaults to the identifier of seg_prep_data() if newdata contains it, otherwise the row number (column row).

labels

Logical. Whether to add the cluster labels of an existing segmentation (seg_as_cluster()) as value labels to cluster. Defaults to TRUE.

verbose

Logical. Whether to report respondents that could not be assigned. Defaults to TRUE.

...

Not used.

Value

A tibble with one row per row of newdata (in the same order), with the identifier, the assigned cluster (NA for respondents who could not be assigned, 0 for noise of density-based methods), the rule-specific information (see "Assignment rules") and, for type = "prob", the membership probabilities.

Details

Preparation of the new data

The new respondents are prepared exactly like the respondents of the solution in seg_prep_data(), using the parameters of the original sample (never statistics of the new data):

  1. The clustering variables are selected from newdata (other columns are ignored) and value labels are removed.

  2. Respondents without any valid answer, or with more missing values than max_missing_prop, are not assigned (NA).

  3. Missing values are handled with the strategy of seg_prep_data():

    • "omit": respondents with missing values are not assigned (NA).

    • "mean" / "median": imputed with the means / medians of the original sample.

    • "mice": the new respondents are appended to the original sample and imputed with mice::mice(), where the imputation model is estimated on the original sample only (argument ignore) and the settings of imputation_args and the seed of seg_prep_data() are reused, so that the imputation is reproducible.

  4. The variables are rescaled with the means and standard deviations (scale = "z") or the minima and ranges (scale = "range") of the original sample.

Assignment rules

Each method assigns new respondents in the way that is consistent with how it formed the clusters (rule = NULL, the default):

  • k-means and hierarchical k-means ("centroid"): the cluster with the nearest center (Euclidean distance), as in the assignment step of k-means. Additional column: distance to that center.

  • PAM ("medoid"): the cluster with the nearest medoid, using the distance measure of seg_prep_data(). Additional column: distance to that medoid.

  • AGNES and DIANA ("linkage"): the cluster the respondent would be merged with first under the linkage of the solution:

    • "ward": the smallest increase of the within-cluster sum of squares, \(\frac{n_c}{n_c + 1}(\bar{d^2}(x, c) - W_c)\), computed from the distances only (for Euclidean distances: the nearest center, weighted by cluster size),

    • "average", "weighted", "gaverage" and DIANA: the smallest average distance to the members of the cluster,

    • "complete": the smallest maximum distance,

    • "single": the nearest member.

    Additional column: distance, the linkage distance (for Ward on the scale of the dendrogram heights).

  • Fuzzy clustering ("membership"): membership degrees that minimize the objective function of cluster::fanny() for the new respondent, with the memberships of the original sample fixed. With the membership exponent \(r\) and \(a_c(x) = \sum_j u_{jc}^r d(x, j) / \sum_j u_{jc}^r - \sum_{i,j} u_{ic}^r u_{jc}^r d(i, j) / (2 (\sum_j u_{jc}^r)^2)\), the membership in cluster \(c\) is proportional to \(a_c(x)^{-1/(r-1)}\). The respondent is assigned to the cluster with the highest membership. Additional column: membership_max.

  • Model-based clustering ("model"): posterior probabilities of the fitted Gaussian mixture model (mclust::predict.Mclust()); the respondent is assigned to the most probable cluster. Additional column: uncertainty (1 - highest probability).

  • DBSCAN ("density"): the cluster of the nearest clustered (non-noise) respondent of the original sample if it lies within eps, otherwise noise (0), as in dbscan::predict().

  • HDBSCAN ("density"): the cluster of the nearest clustered respondent of the original sample if it lies within that respondent's core distance, otherwise noise (0), as in dbscan::predict(). Both density rules use the distance measure of seg_prep_data(). Additional column: distance to the nearest clustered respondent.

  • Existing segmentations from seg_as_cluster() ("centroid").

Two alternative rules can be chosen for every method:

  • rule = "centroid": nearest cluster center (Euclidean distance).

  • rule = "knn": majority vote of the neighbors nearest respondents of the original sample (distance measure of seg_prep_data(); ties are resolved by the smallest summed distance). The share of votes per cluster is returned as probabilities with type = "prob", the highest share as knn_share.

Consistency with the original assignment

Applied to the respondents of the original sample, the rules of k-means, hierarchical k-means, PAM, fuzzy clustering (memberships), model-based clustering (probabilities) and the density-based methods reproduce the original assignment. For AGNES and DIANA, the linkage rule reproduces it for most, but not all respondents (typically 80-90%), as the clusters are formed by successively merging groups and cutting the tree, so that their borders do not follow a simple rule for single respondents. rule = "knn" often agrees more closely with the original assignment of these methods.

With missing = "mice", passing the original sample as newdata re-imputes its missing values, so that respondents with imputed values may be assigned differently. Use newdata = NULL for the original assignment.

See also

Other clustering: seg_agreement(), seg_as_cluster(), seg_cluster(), seg_cluster_density(), seg_cluster_fuzzy(), seg_cluster_hierarchical(), seg_cluster_hkmeans(), seg_cluster_model(), seg_cluster_partitioning(), seg_dbscan_eps(), seg_plot_centers(), seg_plot_cluster(), seg_plot_dend(), seg_plot_heatmap()

Examples

# \donttest{
# Solution on one half of the sample, assignment of the other half
train <- sm_synthetic[1:600, ]
new <- sm_synthetic[601:nrow(sm_synthetic), ]

prep <- seg_prep_data(
  train,
  vars = dplyr::starts_with("F50_0_"),
  id = "id",
  missing = "mean",
  verbose = FALSE
)
cl <- seg_cluster(prep, k = 4, plots = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

pred <- predict(cl, new)
pred
#> # A tibble: 801 × 3
#>       id cluster distance
#>    <dbl>   <int>    <dbl>
#>  1   601       1     3.69
#>  2   602       3     3.32
#>  3   603       2     2.87
#>  4   604       3     2.55
#>  5   605       4     5.57
#>  6   606       1     3.84
#>  7   607       1     3.98
#>  8   608       3     3.45
#>  9   609       2     3.03
#> 10   610       4     3.92
#> # ℹ 791 more rows
table(pred$cluster, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#>   1   2   3   4 
#> 245 183 222 151 

# Membership probabilities of fuzzy clustering
cl_fuzzy <- seg_cluster(prep, "fuzzy", k = 3, plots = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
predict(cl_fuzzy, new, type = "prob")
#> # A tibble: 801 × 6
#>       id cluster membership_max prob_cluster_1 prob_cluster_2 prob_cluster_3
#>    <dbl>   <int>          <dbl>          <dbl>          <dbl>          <dbl>
#>  1   601       1          0.812         0.812         0.0734        0.114

#>  4   604       2          0.981         0.0191        0.981         0.000113

#>  7   607       1          0.655         0.655         0.0199        0.325

#>  9   609       1          0.882         0.882         0.0350        0.0835  
#> 10   610       3          0.951         0.0474        0.00150       0.951   
#> # ℹ 791 more rows

# Alternative rule: 10 nearest neighbors
predict(cl, new, rule = "knn", type = "prob")
#> # A tibble: 801 × 7
#>       id cluster knn_share prob_cluster_1 prob_cluster_2 prob_cluster_3
